newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - ADRS seen surging on bargain-hunting.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - ADRS seen surging on bargain-hunting.

text.p: Foreign companies' American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) should continue their surge into 1997 spurred by bargain-hunting investors, analysts said.
New ADR issues next year are expected to feature a flood of privatizations from Latin America and offerings from telecommunications companies around the world.
Analysts said investors were likely to swing toward foreign companies, including ADRs, as the U.S. bull market made it tougher to find American shares that are relatively undervalued.
"I believe that we're seeing that investors, as the U.S. market is hitting new highs, are getting more cautious," said Amit Khandwala, head of international equities at Wright Investors Service.
"We are seeing that there are more and more reduced positions in equities."

ADRs allow U.S. investors to buy foreign companies' shares in the United States. The top-grade ADRs trade on U.S. exchanges under Securities and Exchange Commission regulations and accounting rules, making them as trustworthy as any U.S. share.

Khandwala and Stephen Dexter, co-manager of Kemper International Equity Funds in Chicago, agreed that European companies in particular were likely to become more attractive in 1997 as they followed the U.S. example and began to streamline operations and stress efficiency.
"They've got a whole new word in Europe now -- shareholders," Dexter said. "Those companies sell at much lower multiples than their equivalents in the United States."

Analysts said that even as investors took a closer look at foreign companies, the number of ADRs being traded in New York is likely to soar next year as companies try to tap into the booming U.S. equity markets.

"We don't see the market slowing down at all worldwide in developed and emerging markets," said Joseph Velli, executive vice president responsible for worldwide securities processing at the Bank of New York, the leading institution handling ADRs.
"We will see 200 new ADRs next year and we also expect trading volume in the U.S. again to grow 30 percent next year. We are very optimistic."
Bankers Trust Co reported that a total of 151 new depositary receipt programs, including ADRs, were established in the first three quarters of 1996, up from 105 in the same period in 1995.

Telecommunications issues were heavily represented among top new ADR offerings in 1996. They included Germany's Deutsche Telekom AG, Venezuela's CANTV and Russia's Vimpel-Communications, the first Russian company to be traded on the New York Stock Exchange.

The top new offerings in 1997 are expected to include privatization of Venezuelan state steel company Sidor, the partial sale of Brazil's phone company Telebras and the start of privatization of such other Brazilian giants as mining company Companhia Vale do Rio Doce and the state power sector.

Other foreign companies likely to test the New York markets with share issues include Italian state telephone group Stet, due to be privatized in late 1997, and France Telecom, the national phone company.
